question: What is the difference between compile-time and runtime errors?

scenes.sub: Caught before the program exists, or after it is already running.
scenes.say: Compile time errors versus runtime errors. The difference is when the mistake is caught, and that changes everything about how bad it is.

scenes.head: Compile-time: the compiler stops you

output.text:
main.cpp:2:13: error: invalid conversion from 'const char*' to 'int'
main.cpp:3:5: error: 'undefinedFn' was not declared in this scope
main.cpp:4:14: error: expected ',' or ';' before '}' token

scenes.say: A compile time error is found by the compiler, before the program ever runs. Wrong types, unknown names, missing semicolons. No executable is produced at all, so this bug can never reach a user. That's the good kind of error.

scenes.head: Runtime: it builds, then fails
scenes.say: A runtime error compiles without complaint, then fails while running, often only for certain inputs. If the user types zero, ten divided by d crashes the program. And asking for element ten of a three element vector with at throws an out of range exception.

scenes.head: A timeline of when bugs show up

items.sub: logic errors: no crash at all

scenes.say: Think of it as a timeline. Compile time errors are caught first, and cheapest. Link errors come next, like a missing definition. Runtime errors only appear while the program runs, maybe only for some inputs, maybe in front of your users. Logic errors are the sneakiest: no crash, just a wrong answer.

scenes.head: Push mistakes toward compile time
scenes.say: Good C plus plus pushes mistakes toward compile time. static assert checks your assumptions while compiling. And strong types, like enum class, turn a wrong argument into a compile error, instead of a bug at runtime.

lines: Compile-time: found by the compiler. Syntax, types, names. No program is built.
Runtime: the program builds, then fails while running. Bad input, bad index, null.
Prefer errors at compile time: strong types, const, static_assert.
scenes.say: Compile time errors are found by the compiler, and no program is built. Runtime errors happen while the program runs, often depending on input. Prefer to catch errors at compile time, using strong types, const, and static assert.
